dx: Eosinophilic esophagitis with food impaction in an atopic teenage boy
case: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after a piece of steak became stuck while he was eating. He cannot swallow his saliva. He has had intermittent dysphagia to solid foods for 2 years. He has asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis. Vital signs are within normal limits. Endoscopy shows a meat bolus lodged in the midesophagus, which is removed. The mucosa shows concentric rings, linear furrows, and white exudates. Biopsies from the proximal and distal esophagus show 45 eosinophils per high-power field (diagnostic threshold, 15 or more). Histology is unchanged after 8 weeks of proton pump inhibitor therapy. Diagnosis: eosinophilic esophagitis.

questions.stem: Before the biopsies were read, reflux esophagitis was also considered. Which of the following findings would have favored reflux esophagitis over eosinophilic esophagitis?
options: Over 15 eosinophils per high-power field proximally
Few eosinophils confined to the distal esophagus
Eosinophil microabscesses with subepithelial fibrosis
Concentric rings and linear furrows on endoscopy
approach: Recall how reflux esophagitis looks on biopsy: basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae, and at most a few eosinophils, limited to the distal esophagus.
Recall eosinophilic esophagitis: 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, often along the whole esophagus, with rings, furrows, and food impaction in an atopic patient.
Pick the finding that fits reflux and not eosinophilic esophagitis.
questions.why: Acid injures the distal esophagus first, so reflux esophagitis shows basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae, and at most a few eosinophils confined to the distal segment, and it improves with acid suppression. Eosinophilic esophagitis is a Th2-driven allergic disease of atopic people. Biopsies from both the proximal and distal esophagus show 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, often with eosinophil microabscesses and fibrosis beneath the epithelium, and endoscopy shows rings, furrows, and white exudates. Pill esophagitis is a third pattern: a focal ulcer where a tablet such as doxycycline, an NSAID, or potassium chloride lodged.
whyNot: Dense eosinophils in the proximal esophagus point to eosinophilic esophagitis, because acid injury is greatest near the gastroesophageal junction.
Correct.
Eosinophil microabscesses and fibrosis beneath the epithelium are features of eosinophilic esophagitis.
Concentric rings and linear furrows are the classic endoscopic findings of eosinophilic esophagitis.

questions.stem: At endoscopy the bolus was lodged about 25 cm from the incisors, at a normal narrowing where the esophagus is indented from its left side at about the T4 to T5 vertebral level. Which of the following structures produce this narrowing?
options: Azygos arch and right main bronchus
Thoracic duct and hemiazygos vein
Right crus of the diaphragm at the hiatus
Aortic arch and left main bronchus
approach: Recall the three normal esophageal narrowings and their distances from the incisors: about 15 cm, about 22 to 27 cm, and about 40 cm.
Match the middle narrowing to the structures that cross the esophagus there.
The left-sided indentation in the upper thorax points to the aortic arch, with the left main bronchus just below it.
questions.why: The esophagus has three normal narrowings. The first is at the cricopharyngeus at about C6, about 15 cm from the incisors. The second is in the thorax, about 22 to 27 cm from the incisors, where the aortic arch and then the left main bronchus cross and indent its left side. The third is at the esophageal hiatus at about T10, about 40 cm from the incisors. Food boluses and swallowed objects tend to lodge at these points, especially when eosinophilic inflammation has already narrowed the lumen.
whyNot: The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus on the right side of the esophagus, and these structures do not form one of the normal narrowings.
The thoracic duct and hemiazygos vein lie behind the esophagus and do not narrow its lumen.
The right crus forms the narrowing at the esophageal hiatus at about T10, about 40 cm from the incisors, where a bolus would lodge at the gastroesophageal junction.
Correct.

topics: Course of the esophagus in the mediastinum

questions.stem: Because intact food proteins drive his disease, he is started on an elemental formula that supplies protein only as free amino acids. Which of the following amino acids must the formula contain because his cells cannot synthesize it?
options: Leucine
Alanine
Aspartate
Serine
approach: Recognize that an elemental formula replaces all dietary protein, so it must supply every essential amino acid.
Recall the nine essential amino acids: phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, and lysine.
Pick the one on that list; the others can be built from glycolytic or citric acid cycle intermediates.
questions.why: Humans cannot make the carbon skeletons of nine amino acids, so they must come from the diet. Leucine, a branched-chain amino acid, is one of them. Alanine comes from transamination of pyruvate, aspartate from transamination of oxaloacetate, and serine from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phosphoglycerate. A formula that leaves out any essential amino acid causes negative nitrogen balance even when total protein intake is adequate.
whyNot: Correct.
Alanine is made from pyruvate by alanine aminotransferase, so the body can supply it.
Aspartate is made from oxaloacetate by aspartate aminotransferase.
Serine is made from 3-phosphoglycerate, an intermediate of glycolysis.

topics: Amino acid synthesis from metabolic intermediates

questions.stem: The neutral amino acids in his formula, such as tryptophan, enter enterocytes through the same apical transporter that is defective in Hartnup disease. Which of the following provides the energy for uptake through this transporter?
options: Proton gradient made by the apical Na+/H+ exchanger 3
ATP hydrolysis by the transporter protein itself
Sodium gradient made by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
Diffusion down the luminal amino acid gradient
approach: Identify the Hartnup transporter (B0AT1, encoded by SLC6A19) as a sodium-coupled neutral amino acid carrier.
Recall that sodium-coupled carriers perform secondary active transport.
Trace the sodium gradient back to the Na+/K+-ATPase on the basolateral membrane.
questions.why: Free neutral amino acids cross the apical membrane together with sodium through B0AT1, the transporter that is defective in Hartnup disease. This is secondary active transport: the carrier uses the inward sodium gradient, which the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase maintains by pumping sodium out of the cell. When the carrier fails, tryptophan is lost in stool and urine, less is available for niacin synthesis, and pellagra-like rash and neurologic findings can appear. Dipeptides and tripeptides use a separate route, the proton-coupled PepT1, so Hartnup patients still absorb some tryptophan from peptides.
whyNot: A proton gradient drives PepT1, which carries dipeptides and tripeptides; free neutral amino acids such as tryptophan use a sodium-coupled carrier.
Carriers that hydrolyze ATP directly are primary active pumps, such as the Na+/K+-ATPase itself; amino acid carriers do not hydrolyze ATP.
Correct.
Diffusion alone could not move amino acids into a cell that already holds them at higher concentration, and much of the formula would go unabsorbed.

dx: Diabetic gastroparesis with persistent vomiting in a woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes
case: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 6 months of early satiety, bloating, and vomiting of food eaten several hours earlier. She has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 22 years with poor glycemic control; her hemoglobin A1c is 9.6% (under 5.7). She also has proliferative retinopathy and burning pain in both feet. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg supine and 98/62 mm Hg standing, with no change in pulse. Upper endoscopy shows retained food in the stomach and no obstruction. Gastric emptying scintigraphy shows 38% retention at 4 hours (normal, under 10%). Diagnosis: diabetic gastroparesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her delayed gastric emptying?
options: Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus
Loss of sympathetic inhibition of gastric smooth muscle
Loss of vagal input that drives antral contractions
Narrowing of the duodenal lumen by fibrosis
approach: Note the setting: long-standing, poorly controlled type 1 diabetes with retinopathy, neuropathy, and a fixed heart rate on standing, all signs of microvascular and autonomic damage.
Endoscopy excludes obstruction, so the delay is a motor problem.
Vagal efferents drive antral contractions and coordinated pyloric relaxation; when they degenerate, the stomach empties slowly.
questions.why: Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. In diabetes, long-standing hyperglycemia damages the vagus nerve, enteric neurons, and interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the stomach. Antral contractions weaken and the pylorus fails to relax in step with them, so solids stay in the stomach for hours, causing early satiety and vomiting of old food. Her fixed heart rate and orthostatic hypotension show that the autonomic neuropathy is widespread.
whyNot: Pyloric muscle hypertrophy causes infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, a mechanical outlet obstruction that endoscopy would show.
Sympathetic input inhibits gastric motility, so losing it would speed emptying.
Correct.
Endoscopy found no obstruction, and a fibrotic duodenal stricture would appear as a narrowed segment.

questions.stem: She is started on low-dose erythromycin, which stimulates receptors for a hormone that is released about every 90 minutes during fasting and triggers strong gastric contractions that sweep undigested solids into the duodenum. Which of the following hormones, with its source cell, does erythromycin mimic?
options: Motilin from M cells
Gastrin from G cells
Secretin from S cells
GIP from K cells
approach: Identify the fasting motor pattern as the migrating motor complex, whose phase III contractions clear residue from the stomach.
Recall that motilin, from M cells of the duodenum and jejunum, rises during fasting and starts phase III.
Erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist, so it speeds gastric emptying.
questions.why: Between meals, the stomach and small intestine cycle through the migrating motor complex about every 90 to 120 minutes. Motilin from M cells in the upper small intestine peaks with phase III, a burst of strong contractions that sweeps indigestible solids out of the stomach and along the small bowel. Eating suppresses motilin release and stops the cycle. Erythromycin binds motilin receptors and triggers these contractions, which is why it is used short term for gastroparesis.
whyNot: Correct.
Gastrin from antral G cells responds to peptides and vagal stimulation after a meal and mainly increases acid secretion.
Secretin from S cells responds to acid in the duodenum, releases pancreatic bicarbonate, and slows gastric emptying.
GIP from K cells responds to glucose and fat in the duodenum and mainly increases insulin release.

topics: Motilin and the migrating motor complex

questions.stem: A full-thickness gastric biopsy shows loss of neurons in the myenteric plexus and fewer interstitial cells of Cajal. The myenteric neurons she lost developed from which of the following embryonic sources?
options: Splanchnic mesoderm
Foregut endoderm
Basal plate of the neural tube
Vagal neural crest cells
approach: Separate the cell types: enteric neurons and glia versus smooth muscle and interstitial cells of Cajal.
Recall that enteric neurons come from neural crest cells, mostly from the vagal (hindbrain) level, which migrate into the gut wall.
Smooth muscle and interstitial cells of Cajal come from splanchnic mesoderm, and the epithelium from endoderm.
questions.why: The myenteric and submucosal plexuses form from neural crest cells, mostly vagal crest cells from the hindbrain region, that enter the foregut and migrate along the gut from cranial to caudal. They become enteric neurons and glia. RET signaling is required for this migration, and failure to reach the distal colon leaves the aganglionic segment of Hirschsprung disease. The interstitial cells of Cajal and smooth muscle layers come from splanchnic mesoderm, and the mucosal epithelium comes from endoderm.
whyNot: Splanchnic mesoderm forms the smooth muscle, connective tissue, and interstitial cells of Cajal of the gut wall, but not its neurons.
Foregut endoderm forms the epithelium and glands of the stomach.
The basal plate of the neural tube forms motor neurons of the spinal cord and brainstem, including the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, which lie outside the gut wall.
Correct.

topics: Development of the enteric nervous system

questions.stem: To ease her symptoms, she ate almost no fruits or vegetables for several months. She now has bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and coiled hairs on her legs. Reduced activity of which of the following enzymes most directly explains these findings?
options: Copper-dependent lysyl oxidase
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases
Gamma-glutamyl carboxylase
Procollagen N-proteinase
approach: Link the diet without fruits or vegetables and the findings (gum bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs) to vitamin C deficiency.
Recall that ascorbate keeps the iron of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the reduced ferrous state.
Without hydroxylation, collagen triple helices are unstable, so vessel walls and gums become fragile.
questions.why: Vitamin C is the cofactor that keeps the iron in prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases reduced, so they can hydroxylate proline and lysine residues of procollagen in the endoplasmic reticulum. Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix through hydrogen bonds, and hydroxylysine is needed for later cross-linking. Without vitamin C, collagen is weak, small vessels rupture, and scurvy appears with gum bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, and poor wound healing. Symptoms can develop within about 1 to 3 months of a diet lacking fresh fruits and vegetables.
whyNot: Lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen and elastin outside the cell using copper; it fails in Menkes disease and copper deficiency.
Correct.
Gamma-glutamyl carboxylase needs vitamin K and activates clotting factors; its failure causes bleeding with a prolonged PT, without hair or follicle changes.
Procollagen N-proteinase removes the amino-terminal propeptides outside the cell; its inherited defect causes the dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

dx: Sigmoid volvulus in an older nursing home resident with chronic constipation
case: An 81-year-old man who lives in a nursing home is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of increasing abdominal distension and no passage of stool or flatus. He has Parkinson disease and long-standing constipation treated with laxatives. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. The abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with mild diffuse tenderness. Digital rectal examination shows hard stool in the rectal vault. An abdominal radiograph shows a greatly dilated, inverted U-shaped loop of colon rising from the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant, with no free air. Diagnosis: sigmoid volvulus.

questions.stem: Which of the following anatomic features most likely allowed this segment of bowel to twist?
options: Long sigmoid mesocolon with a narrow base
Hypertrophied lymphoid tissue acting as a lead point
Narrow small bowel mesentery from malrotation
Polypoid tumor pulled forward by peristalsis
approach: Recognize volvulus as a twist of bowel around its own mesentery, which needs a mobile loop on a narrow pedicle.
Recall that in older adults the sigmoid is the usual site, especially with chronic constipation that lengthens and loads the loop.
Separate this from intussusception, which needs a lead point that peristalsis pulls into the next segment.
questions.why: Sigmoid volvulus occurs when a long, redundant sigmoid loop twists on a mesocolon that is narrow at its base. Chronic constipation, laxative use, neurologic disease, and institutional living lengthen and load the loop, so older nursing home residents are the classic patients. The twist closes the lumen at two points, creating a closed loop, and kinks the mesenteric vessels, so the loop can become ischemic. In infants, volvulus usually involves the midgut and follows malrotation, and intussusception is the main telescoping disorder of young children.
whyNot: Correct.
Hypertrophied Peyer patches act as a lead point for ileocolic intussusception in young children, often after a viral illness.
A narrow small bowel mesentery from malrotation causes midgut volvulus, usually in newborns with bilious vomiting.
A polypoid tumor acting as a lead point causes intussusception in adults, where the bowel telescopes into the next segment instead of twisting.

questions.stem: His sigmoid colon twisted, while the descending colon just above it cannot twist. Which of the following organs is held in place for the same reason as the descending colon?
options: Transverse colon
Stomach
Pancreatic head
Jejunum
approach: Ask why the descending colon cannot twist: it lost its mesentery during development and fused to the posterior abdominal wall, so it is secondarily retroperitoneal.
Recall the other secondarily retroperitoneal structures: duodenal parts 2 to 4, the ascending colon, and the pancreas except its tail.
Pick the pancreatic head; the other options keep a mesentery or peritoneal ligaments and stay mobile.
questions.why: During development the ascending and descending colon press against the posterior abdominal wall, and their mesenteries fuse with the parietal peritoneum. They become secondarily retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on their front and sides, and cannot rotate. The head, neck, and body of the pancreas and duodenal parts 2 to 4 become fixed in the same way. The transverse and sigmoid colon keep their mesenteries, stay intraperitoneal, and remain mobile, which is why volvulus affects the sigmoid.
whyNot: The transverse colon hangs from the transverse mesocolon and is intraperitoneal, so it is mobile and can occasionally twist.
The stomach is intraperitoneal and held only by the omenta and peritoneal ligaments, so it can twist, as in gastric volvulus.
Correct.
The jejunum is intraperitoneal and suspended by the mesentery of the small intestine.

questions.stem: As part of his bowel regimen, nursing staff help him to the toilet about 20 minutes after breakfast each day. Which of the following physiologic responses does this timing take advantage of?
options: Enterogastric reflex speeding gastric emptying
Gastrocolic reflex increasing colonic mass movements
Rectoanal inhibitory reflex relaxing the external sphincter
Migrating motor complex clearing the fed colon
approach: Note the timing: shortly after a meal.
Recall that stretch of the stomach after eating triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which increases colonic motility and mass movements within minutes.
Mass movements push stool into the rectum, and rectal distension then starts the urge to defecate.
questions.why: When food stretches the stomach, the gastrocolic reflex increases colonic motility within minutes. It is carried by enteric and extrinsic parasympathetic nerves, helped by hormones such as gastrin and CCK. The resulting mass movements push stool into the rectum, and rectal distension starts the defecation reflex: the internal anal sphincter relaxes reflexly and the external sphincter relaxes under voluntary control. Scheduled toileting after meals uses this reflex and is a standard part of bowel care for older adults with constipation.
whyNot: The enterogastric reflex slows gastric emptying when acid, fat, or distension reaches the duodenum.
Correct.
The rectoanal inhibitory reflex relaxes the internal anal sphincter in response to rectal distension; the external sphincter is under voluntary control through the pudendal nerve.
The migrating motor complex runs during fasting, mainly in the stomach and small intestine, and stops when a meal is eaten.

questions.stem: His colonic dilation is acquired. Which of the following findings would most suggest Hirschsprung disease as the cause of megacolon in a different patient?
options: Fever, bloody diarrhea, and a colon over 6 cm on radiograph
Dysphagia and cardiomyopathy in a man raised in rural Brazil
Hard stool packing the rectal vault on digital examination
Meconium passage after 48 hours with an empty rectal vault
approach: List the main causes of megacolon: Hirschsprung disease, Chagas disease, toxic megacolon, and chronic acquired constipation.
Recall Hirschsprung features: absent ganglion cells in the rectum, so the newborn cannot pass meconium and the contracted rectum stays empty while stool builds up above it.
Match each other option to its cause and exclude it.
questions.why: In Hirschsprung disease, neural crest cells fail to reach the distal bowel, so the rectum and a variable length of colon lack ganglion cells and stay contracted. Stool cannot pass the aganglionic segment, and the colon above it dilates. Most affected newborns fail to pass meconium in the first 48 hours, and the rectal vault is empty on examination, often followed by an explosive release of stool when the examining finger is withdrawn. In acquired megacolon from chronic constipation, like this patient's, the rectum is usually packed with stool.
whyNot: Fever, bloody diarrhea, and acute colonic dilation point to toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis or Clostridioides difficile colitis.
Dysphagia, cardiomyopathy, and megacolon in someone from rural Latin America suggest Chagas disease, in which Trypanosoma cruzi infection destroys enteric ganglion cells.
A rectum packed with hard stool fits chronic acquired constipation, as in this patient, in which the rectal wall has ganglion cells and the vault fills with stool.
Correct.

dx: Midgut volvulus from intestinal malrotation in a newborn
case: A 3-day-old girl is evaluated in the newborn nursery because of repeated green vomiting that began 6 hours ago. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and passed meconium on the first day of life. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 176/min, respirations are 48/min, and blood pressure is 62/38 mm Hg. The abdomen is mildly distended and tender. An abdominal radiograph shows a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum with scattered gas in the distal small bowel. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study shows the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the midline and a corkscrew appearance of the distal duodenum. At surgery, the midgut is twisted around a narrow mesenteric base. Diagnosis: midgut volvulus due to intestinal malrotation.

questions.stem: Failure of which of the following developmental events most directly explains the position of the duodenojejunal junction in this infant?
options: Return of the herniated midgut into the abdomen
Recanalization of the solid duodenal lumen
Obliteration of the vitelline duct at the umbilicus
Full counterclockwise rotation of the midgut loop
approach: Note that the duodenojejunal junction lies right of the midline, so the gut did not complete its rotation.
Recall that the midgut loop rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery while it herniates in week 6 and returns by week 10.
Incomplete rotation leaves a narrow mesenteric base and peritoneal bands, which predispose to volvulus.
questions.why: During week 6 the midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord and begins rotating counterclockwise, viewed from the front, around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. It completes about 270 degrees of rotation as it returns to the abdomen by about week 10, which places the duodenojejunal junction left of the midline and the cecum in the right lower quadrant. In malrotation the rotation is incomplete, so the duodenojejunal junction stays on the right and the mesentery has a narrow base that twists easily. Peritoneal (Ladd) bands from the malpositioned cecum can also cross and compress the duodenum.
whyNot: Failed return of the herniated midgut leaves bowel in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus, an omphalocele.
Failed recanalization causes duodenal atresia, with no gas beyond the duodenum.
Persistence of the vitelline duct causes a Meckel diverticulum or a vitelline fistula and does not change the position of the duodenum.
Correct.

questions.stem: Duodenal atresia was considered before the contrast study was done. Which of the following findings in this infant most strongly argued against duodenal atresia?
options: Green color of the vomitus
Gas in the distal small bowel
Dilated stomach and proximal duodenum
Onset of vomiting in the first week
approach: Recall the classic radiograph of duodenal atresia: a double bubble with no gas beyond the duodenum.
Recognize that atresia is a complete block, so swallowed air cannot reach the distal bowel.
Gas in the distal bowel means the duodenum is at least partly open, which fits volvulus or another partial obstruction.
questions.why: Duodenal atresia results from failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize after it is temporarily filled by proliferating epithelium during the second month. The block is complete, so the radiograph shows a double bubble, gas in the stomach and proximal duodenum, with no gas beyond. Because most atresias lie below the ampulla, the vomitus is bilious, and the condition is strongly associated with Down syndrome. In midgut volvulus the obstruction is often partial at first, so some gas reaches the distal bowel. Bilious vomiting in a newborn with distal gas still needs urgent study for malrotation.
whyNot: Bilious vomiting occurs in both conditions, because most duodenal atresias lie below the entry of the bile duct.
Correct.
A dilated stomach and proximal duodenum form the double bubble, which is expected in duodenal atresia.
Duodenal atresia usually causes vomiting within the first day or two of life, so early onset fits it.

questions.stem: If the twist is not relieved, which of the following patterns of bowel injury is most likely?
options: Mucosal infarction at the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid
Necrosis of a single loop trapped in an inguinal hernia
Transmural infarction from jejunum to mid transverse colon
Infarction of the stomach and first part of the duodenum
approach: Recognize that the midgut twists around the superior mesenteric artery and vein, so the volvulus occludes both.
Map the territory of the superior mesenteric artery: distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, ascending colon, and the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
Complete occlusion of a major artery causes transmural infarction, as in acute mesenteric ischemia from an embolus in adults.
questions.why: Midgut volvulus twists the bowel around the superior mesenteric vessels. Venous outflow is blocked first and arterial inflow soon after, so the whole territory of the superior mesenteric artery becomes ischemic within hours. Without prompt surgery the result is transmural hemorrhagic infarction of most of the small bowel and the right and proximal transverse colon, with bloody stool, rising lactate, and shock. This mirrors acute mesenteric ischemia in adults, in which an embolus from atrial fibrillation lodges in the superior mesenteric artery. Chronic mesenteric ischemia causes postprandial pain and weight loss, and ischemic colitis affects watershed regions of the colon.
whyNot: Mucosal injury at the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction is ischemic colitis from low flow in watershed areas, usually in older adults with hypotension.
Necrosis of a single trapped loop fits a strangulated abdominal wall hernia.
Correct.
The stomach and proximal duodenum are foregut structures supplied by the celiac trunk, which a midgut twist spares.

questions.stem: Her vomiting is triggered by distension of the obstructed duodenum. Which of the following pathways most directly carries this stimulus to start vomiting?
options: Vagal afferents to the medullary vomiting center
Blood-borne signals to the area postrema
Vestibular nerve input to the vestibular nuclei
Spinothalamic fibers to the somatosensory cortex
approach: Identify the stimulus: stretch of the gut wall, sensed by visceral afferents.
Recall that gut distension signals travel in vagal afferents to the nucleus tractus solitarius and the vomiting center in the medulla.
Reserve the area postrema for blood-borne triggers such as drugs, toxins, and uremia.
questions.why: Vomiting is coordinated by neurons in the medulla, often called the vomiting center, closely linked to the nucleus tractus solitarius. Distension or irritation of the stomach and duodenum is sensed by vagal afferents, which project directly to this region. The chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema lies outside the blood-brain barrier, responds to chemicals in the blood, and relays to the same center. Prolonged vomiting of gastric contents causes hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
whyNot: Correct.
The area postrema chemoreceptor trigger zone mainly detects blood-borne emetic agents, such as chemotherapy drugs, opioids, and uremic toxins.
Vestibular input causes motion sickness through the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.
Spinothalamic fibers carry somatic pain and temperature to the cortex and do not start the vomiting reflex.

dx: Postoperative paralytic ileus with hypokalemia after colectomy
case: A 63-year-old woman is evaluated on the fourth day after open sigmoid colectomy for recurrent diverticulitis because of abdominal distension, nausea, and no passage of flatus or stool. She has received intravenous morphine for pain and has had about 1.5 L/day of nasogastric drainage. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. The abdomen is distended and mildly tender around the incision, and bowel sounds are absent. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0). An abdominal radiograph shows gas-filled, dilated loops of both small and large bowel without a transition point. Diagnosis: postoperative paralytic ileus with hypokalemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how her low serum potassium contributes to her ileus?
options: Persistent depolarization that inactivates sodium channels
Hyperpolarized smooth muscle that resists excitation
Increased acetylcholine release from enteric neurons
Enhanced mu-opioid signaling in the myenteric plexus
approach: Recall that the resting membrane potential depends mainly on the potassium gradient.
Low extracellular potassium makes the potassium equilibrium potential more negative, so smooth muscle cells hyperpolarize.
Hyperpolarized cells reach threshold less often, so slow waves trigger fewer spike potentials and contractions weaken.
questions.why: The resting membrane potential of gut smooth muscle is set largely by potassium. When extracellular potassium falls, the potassium equilibrium potential becomes more negative and the cells hyperpolarize. Slow waves then fail to reach the threshold for spike potentials, so contractions are weak or absent. In this patient, hypokalemia from nasogastric losses adds to the other causes of postoperative ileus: handling of the bowel, inflammation, sympathetic activation, and opioids. Absent bowel sounds and gas throughout the small and large bowel with no transition point fit adynamic ileus; mechanical obstruction gives high-pitched bowel sounds and a transition point.
whyNot: Persistent depolarization with sodium channel inactivation is the effect of severe hyperkalemia.
Correct.
More acetylcholine would increase contractions; low potassium lowers the excitability of the muscle itself.
Opioids slow motility through mu receptors in the myenteric plexus, and the serum potassium level does not change this signaling.

questions.stem: Fourteen months later she has colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and high-pitched bowel sounds. CT shows dilated small bowel loops that change abruptly in caliber at a band near her old incision. Which of the following changes in the peritoneum after her surgery most favored formation of this band?
options: Reduced fibrinolytic activity of injured mesothelium
Deposition of immune complexes on the serosa
Eosinophilic infiltration of the visceral peritoneum
Squamous metaplasia of the injured mesothelial lining
approach: Recognize adhesive small bowel obstruction: prior laparotomy, colicky pain, high-pitched bowel sounds, and a transition point.
Recall that surgery injures the mesothelium and leaves a fibrin exudate between peritoneal surfaces.
Healthy mesothelium dissolves this fibrin with plasminogen activator; when that activity is low, fibroblasts invade the fibrin and lay down a permanent collagen band.
questions.why: Handling, drying, ischemia, and inflammation of the peritoneum during surgery produce a fibrin-rich exudate that glues adjacent surfaces together. Healthy mesothelium releases tissue plasminogen activator, which breaks down this fibrin within days. Injured or ischemic mesothelium releases less plasminogen activator and more plasminogen activator inhibitor, so the fibrin persists and is invaded by fibroblasts and small vessels, becoming a fibrous adhesion. Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.
whyNot: Correct.
Immune complex deposition is a feature of type III hypersensitivity, as in lupus serositis, and plays no main part in postoperative adhesions.
Eosinophils in the serosa suggest parasitic or allergic disease, which has no role in surgical healing of the peritoneum.
Injured mesothelium repairs itself by regrowth of mesothelial cells, and adhesion bands are made by fibroblasts laying down collagen.

questions.stem: On postoperative day 8 she develops fever and generalized peritonitis from an anastomotic leak. She has spent most of the past week lying supine in bed. In which of the following upper abdominal spaces is pus most likely to collect?
options: Omental bursa
Left subphrenic space
Infracolic space
Hepatorenal recess
approach: Note her position: supine for days.
Recall that in the supine position the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch) is the lowest part of the upper abdominal cavity.
Fluid from the pelvis and lower abdomen reaches it through the right paracolic gutter, while the phrenicocolic ligament limits flow up the left gutter.
questions.why: Free fluid, pus, or blood in the peritoneal cavity moves to the lowest available space. When a patient lies supine, the hepatorenal recess, between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney, is the most dependent part of the upper abdomen. The right paracolic gutter connects it with the pelvis, while the phrenicocolic ligament limits upward flow on the left. In an upright patient, fluid collects instead in the rectouterine pouch in women and the rectovesical pouch in men, and abscesses form at those sites.
whyNot: The omental bursa (lesser sac) lies behind the stomach and fills mainly from disease of nearby organs, such as pancreatitis or a perforated posterior gastric ulcer.
The left subphrenic space can collect pus after splenic or gastric surgery, but it is less dependent than the hepatorenal recess in a supine patient.
The infracolic spaces drain toward the pelvis and paracolic gutters and are less dependent than the hepatorenal recess when the patient lies flat.
Correct.

topics: Peritoneal recesses and spread of fluid

questions.stem: Assume instead that her ileus had lasted 3 weeks with no caloric intake and no parenteral nutrition. Which of the following adaptations most reduces breakdown of her muscle protein by that time?
options: Liver release of glucose from stored glycogen
Muscle export of free glucose from its own glycogen stores
Brain oxidation of ketone bodies made by the liver
Red cell oxidation of fatty acids for ATP
approach: Recall the timeline: liver glycogen is largely used up within about 24 to 48 hours of fasting, and gluconeogenesis from amino acids then supplies glucose.
Over weeks of starvation, the liver converts fatty acids into ketone bodies, and the brain adapts to use them for much of its energy.
Less glucose demand by the brain means less muscle protein must be broken down for gluconeogenesis.
questions.why: Early in a fast the liver maintains blood glucose by glycogenolysis, then by gluconeogenesis from alanine, lactate, and glycerol, and much of that alanine comes from muscle protein. As fasting continues, fatty acids released from adipose tissue are converted in liver mitochondria to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. After about 2 to 3 weeks the brain meets roughly two-thirds of its energy needs from these ketone bodies. This cuts its glucose requirement, so less muscle protein is broken down to make glucose.
whyNot: Liver glycogen lasts only about a day or two of fasting, so it cannot supply glucose after 3 weeks.
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it uses its glycogen only for its own needs and cannot release free glucose into the blood.
Correct.
Red blood cells lack mitochondria and depend entirely on anaerobic glycolysis of glucose.

dx: Paraesophageal hiatal hernia with gastric volvulus in an older woman
case: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of severe epigastric and lower chest pain for 4 hours, with repeated retching that brings up little material. For several years she has had fullness in the chest after meals and occasional heartburn. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 142/84 mm Hg. Attempts to pass a nasogastric tube fail. A chest radiograph shows a large retrocardiac air-fluid level. CT shows most of the stomach in the posterior mediastinum, rotated around its long axis. Diagnosis: paraesophageal hiatal hernia with acute gastric volvulus.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of her hernia best distinguishes it from the most common type of hiatal hernia?
options: Gastroesophageal junction moves up into the thorax
Hernia passes through a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect
Gastroesophageal junction remains below the diaphragm
Hernia passes through a defect behind the sternum
approach: Recall the two main hiatal hernia types.
In a sliding hernia, about 95% of cases, the gastroesophageal junction itself slides up through the hiatus.
In a paraesophageal hernia, the junction stays in place and the fundus or more of the stomach rolls up beside the esophagus, which can lead to volvulus and strangulation.
questions.why: A sliding hiatal hernia moves the gastroesophageal junction and cardia up into the thorax and mainly causes reflux. A paraesophageal hernia keeps the junction below the diaphragm while the fundus, and sometimes most of the stomach, rolls up through the hiatus beside the esophagus. These hernias cause fewer reflux symptoms but carry a risk of incarceration, gastric volvulus, and strangulation as venous congestion progresses to arterial compromise. Severe pain, retching with little vomitus, and failure to pass a nasogastric tube are the classic triad of acute gastric volvulus.
whyNot: Upward movement of the gastroesophageal junction defines a sliding hernia, the most common type, which mainly causes reflux.
A posterolateral defect is a Bochdalek hernia, a congenital diaphragmatic hernia that usually presents in newborns with respiratory distress.
Correct.
A retrosternal defect is a Morgagni hernia, a rare congenital hernia through the gap between the sternal and costal parts of the diaphragm.

questions.stem: At surgery the stomach is reduced, and its greater curvature is mobilized near the fundus by dividing the ligament that connects it to the hilum of the spleen. Which of the following vessels must be ligated in this ligament?
options: Left gastric artery
Splenic artery and vein
Paraumbilical veins
Short gastric arteries
approach: Name the ligament: the gastrosplenic ligament joins the greater curvature to the splenic hilum.
Recall its contents: the short gastric vessels and the left gastroepiploic vessels.
Separate it from the splenorenal ligament, which carries the splenic artery and vein and the tail of the pancreas.
questions.why: The gastrosplenic ligament is part of the dorsal mesogastrium between the greater curvature of the stomach and the spleen. It carries the short gastric arteries and veins, which run from the splenic vessels to the fundus, and the left gastroepiploic vessels. The splenorenal ligament, from the spleen to the left kidney, carries the splenic artery and vein and the tail of the pancreas. The gastrohepatic ligament carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature, and the falciform ligament carries the ligamentum teres and paraumbilical veins.
whyNot: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature within the gastrohepatic ligament.
The splenic artery and vein run in the splenorenal ligament with the tail of the pancreas.
The paraumbilical veins run in the falciform ligament with the ligamentum teres.
Correct.

topics: Peritoneal ligaments of the stomach and spleen
Blood supply of the gastric fundus

questions.stem: The rotation of her stomach stretches the artery that runs along the upper part of the lesser curvature and also gives branches to the distal esophagus. This artery arises directly from which of the following vessels?
options: Celiac trunk
Common hepatic artery
Splenic artery
Superior mesenteric artery
approach: Identify the artery: the left gastric artery supplies the upper lesser curvature and sends esophageal branches to the distal esophagus.
Recall the three branches of the celiac trunk: left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic.
The left gastric is the smallest of the three and arises directly from the trunk.
questions.why: The celiac trunk leaves the aorta at about T12 and divides into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries. The left gastric artery runs up toward the gastroesophageal junction, gives esophageal branches, and then follows the upper lesser curvature, where it joins the right gastric artery. The splenic artery supplies the fundus and greater curvature through short gastric and left gastroepiploic branches. The common hepatic artery gives the gastroduodenal artery, the vessel eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer, and the proper hepatic artery.
whyNot: Correct.
The common hepatic artery gives the gastroduodenal and proper hepatic arteries; the right gastric artery, which supplies the lower lesser curvature, usually comes from the proper hepatic artery.
The splenic artery supplies the fundus and greater curvature through the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries.
The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, from the distal duodenum to the proximal transverse colon, and does not supply the lesser curvature.

questions.stem: Years earlier, esophageal manometry done for her heartburn showed normal resting pressure in the lower esophageal sphincter. Which of the following mechanisms most likely caused most of her reflux episodes at that time?
options: Sustained gastric acid hypersecretion driven by excess gastrin
Transient sphincter relaxations not triggered by swallowing
Absent peristalsis in the esophageal body
Failure of the sphincter to relax with swallowing
approach: Note that resting sphincter pressure was normal, so a constantly weak sphincter was not the main problem.
Recall that most reflux episodes in GERD occur during transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, which are vagally mediated and triggered by stretch of the stomach rather than by swallowing.
Gastric distension after meals, obesity, and a hiatal hernia make these relaxations more frequent and more likely to let acid reflux.
questions.why: Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations are brief, vagally mediated relaxations that occur without a swallow, usually triggered by stretch of the proximal stomach after a meal. They are how the sphincter vents swallowed air, and they account for most reflux episodes in people with GERD and normal resting sphincter pressure. A low resting sphincter tone and a hiatal hernia, which separates the sphincter from the crural diaphragm, add to reflux in more severe disease. Long-standing reflux can cause chronic cough, hoarseness, peptic stricture, and Barrett esophagus.
whyNot: Acid hypersecretion from excess gastrin occurs in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome; most patients with GERD secrete normal amounts of acid.
Correct.
Absent peristalsis, as in scleroderma, slows clearance of refluxed acid from the esophagus, while the reflux episodes themselves still require the sphincter to open.
Failure of the sphincter to relax with swallowing is achalasia, which causes dysphagia and food retention.

dx: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with cholangiocarcinoma in a man with ulcerative colitis
case: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 months of generalized itching, dark urine, pale stools, and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He has had ulcerative colitis for 15 years. He is jaundiced, and the abdomen is nontender. Laboratory studies show a total bilirubin of 7.4 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin of 6.1 mg/dL (0 to 0.3), alkaline phosphatase of 690 U/L (40 to 130), and ALT of 88 U/L (7 to 56). Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography shows multifocal strictures and dilations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, with a dominant stricture at the hepatic duct bifurcation. Brushings from the stricture show adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis: primary sclerosing cholangitis complicated by perihilar cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from an area away from the tumor is reviewed. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Concentric periductal fibrosis around bile ducts
Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular bile ducts
Interface hepatitis rich in plasma cells
Ground-glass hepatocytes with abundant HBsAg
approach: Link ulcerative colitis, cholestatic laboratory values, and beaded ducts on MRCP to primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Recall the lesion of PSC: inflammation and concentric onion-skin fibrosis around medium and large ducts, which narrows and then obliterates them.
Contrast it with primary biliary cholangitis, which destroys small intrahepatic ducts with granulomas in middle-aged women.
questions.why: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Around affected ducts, collagen is laid down in concentric layers (onion-skin fibrosis), and ducts are eventually replaced by fibrous scars. Alternating strictures and dilated segments give the beaded pattern on cholangiography. PSC is more common in men, is strongly linked to ulcerative colitis, and raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Primary biliary cholangitis affects mostly middle-aged women, is marked by antimitochondrial antibodies, and shows granulomatous destruction of small interlobular ducts.
whyNot: Correct.
Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular ducts is the florid duct lesion of primary biliary cholangitis, which mostly affects middle-aged women with antimitochondrial antibodies.
Interface hepatitis with many plasma cells is typical of autoimmune hepatitis, which raises aminotransferases more than alkaline phosphatase.
Ground-glass hepatocytes filled with HBsAg indicate chronic hepatitis B infection.

questions.stem: In parts of East Asia, the same type of tumor often arises in people without sclerosing cholangitis. Which of the following exposures most likely explains its frequency there?
options: Dietary aflatoxin B1 from moldy stored grain and peanuts
Chronic biliary infection by Clonorchis sinensis
Chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection
Long-term oral contraceptive use
approach: Name the tumor: cholangiocarcinoma, a malignancy of bile duct epithelium.
Recall its two classic risk factors: primary sclerosing cholangitis in Western patients and liver flukes in East and Southeast Asia.
Liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis, acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater fish, live in the bile ducts and keep the epithelium inflamed for years.
questions.why: Cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile duct epithelium after long-standing inflammation of the ducts. In Western countries the main risk factor is primary sclerosing cholangitis. In East and Southeast Asia, chronic infection with the liver flukes Clonorchis sinensis and Opisthorchis viverrini, acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish, keeps the duct epithelium inflamed and proliferating. Perihilar tumors usually present with painless obstructive jaundice, itching, and weight loss, as in this patient.
whyNot: Aflatoxin B1 causes TP53 mutations in hepatocytes and is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, especially with hepatitis B.
Correct.
Schistosoma haematobium lives in the venous plexus of the bladder and causes squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
Oral contraceptives are linked to hepatocellular adenoma, a benign tumor of hepatocytes.

questions.stem: Before imaging, autoantibody tests were sent to look for other autoimmune causes of liver disease. Which of the following results, if positive, would have pointed to primary biliary cholangitis instead?
options: Anti-smooth muscle antibody
Anti-LKM1 antibody
Antimitochondrial antibody
Anti-intrinsic factor antibody
approach: Place PBC among the cholestatic diseases that can resemble PSC.

Recall the marker antibody for each autoimmune GI disease: PBC, antimitochondrial; autoimmune hepatitis type 1, ANA and anti-smooth muscle; type 2, anti-LKM1; autoimmune gastritis, anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor.
Choose the antibody that marks PBC.
questions.why: Antimitochondrial antibody, directed at the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, is present in about 90 to 95% of people with primary biliary cholangitis and is its key serologic marker. Primary sclerosing cholangitis has no specific autoantibody, although p-ANCA is often present. Autoimmune hepatitis is marked by ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody in type 1 and by anti-LKM1 in type 2. Antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor mark autoimmune gastritis and pernicious anemia.
whyNot: Anti-smooth muscle antibody, together with ANA, supports type 1 autoimmune hepatitis.
Anti-LKM1, directed against cytochrome P450 2D6, supports type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, which mostly affects children and young women.
Correct.
Anti-intrinsic factor antibody marks autoimmune gastritis with pernicious anemia and has no role in liver disease.

questions.stem: Review of his records shows that during 4 earlier years of cholestasis he developed loss of vibration and position sense in both feet, a wide-based gait, and a mild hemolytic anemia. Loss of which of the following vitamin functions most likely explains these findings?
options: Gamma-carboxylation of clotting factor glutamates
Formation of rhodopsin in retinal rods
Promotion of intestinal calcium absorption
Protection of membrane lipids from peroxidation
approach: Link cholestasis to fat malabsorption: without bile acids in the gut, vitamins A, D, E, and K are poorly absorbed.
Match the findings, dorsal column and spinocerebellar signs plus hemolysis, to vitamin E deficiency.
Recall that vitamin E is the main lipid-soluble antioxidant in cell membranes.
questions.why: Bile acids form the micelles that carry fat-soluble vitamins into enterocytes, so long-standing cholestasis causes deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K. Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) sits in cell membranes and stops chain reactions of lipid peroxidation by free radicals. Without it, red cell membranes are damaged and hemolysis follows, and long axons in the dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts degenerate, causing loss of vibration and position sense and ataxia. These findings can resemble vitamin B12 deficiency, but vitamin E deficiency does not cause megaloblastic anemia.
whyNot: Gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X needs vitamin K; its loss prolongs the PT and causes bleeding.
Vitamin A forms retinal, part of rhodopsin; its loss causes night blindness and dry eyes.
Vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption; its loss causes osteomalacia with bone pain and weakness.
Correct.

dx: Choledocholithiasis with acute ascending cholangitis and pyogenic liver abscess
case: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of 2 days of right upper quadrant pain, shaking chills, and yellow eyes. Gallstones were found 1 year ago, after she received 10 weeks of total parenteral nutrition while recovering from major trauma. Temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg. She is jaundiced and has right upper quadrant tenderness. Leukocyte count is 19,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000), total bilirubin is 5.8 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), and alkaline phosphatase is 410 U/L (40 to 130). Ultrasonography shows gallstones and a common bile duct dilated to 12 mm (normal, about 6 or less) with a distal stone. CT shows a 5-cm multiloculated abscess in the right hepatic lobe. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Diagnosis: choledocholithiasis with acute cholangitis and pyogenic liver abscess.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings would most strongly indicate that her stone has impacted at the ampulla, where the bile duct and main pancreatic duct share a common channel?
options: Air in the biliary tree with a stone in the distal ileum
Painless, palpable, nontender distended gallbladder
Colicky pain after fatty meals that resolves in hours
Epigastric pain radiating to the back with high lipase
approach: Predict each stone's effect from where it lodges.
A stone blocking the common channel at the ampulla obstructs pancreatic outflow as well as bile, which triggers acute pancreatitis.
Pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal.
questions.why: The consequence of a gallstone depends on where it lodges. In the cystic duct it causes biliary colic or acute cholecystitis. In the common bile duct it causes obstructive jaundice, and infection of the stagnant bile causes ascending cholangitis with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, as in this patient. At the ampulla, where the bile and pancreatic ducts often share a common channel, it also blocks pancreatic drainage and causes gallstone pancreatitis. A large stone that erodes from the gallbladder into the bowel can obstruct the ileum, producing gallstone ileus with air in the biliary tree.
whyNot: Air in the biliary tree with a stone in the ileum describes gallstone ileus from a cholecystoenteric fistula.

A painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice suggests malignant obstruction of the distal duct, such as pancreatic head cancer; gallstone disease usually leaves a scarred gallbladder that cannot distend.
Brief pain after meals that resolves within hours is biliary colic from a stone transiently blocking the cystic duct.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organism and route that most likely produced her liver abscess?
options: Entamoeba histolytica carried by the portal vein from the colon
Staphylococcus aureus seeded through the hepatic artery
Escherichia coli ascending through obstructed bile ducts
Echinococcus granulosus larvae carried from the small intestine
approach: Note the setting: an obstructed, infected bile duct and blood cultures growing a gram-negative enteric rod.
Recall that pyogenic liver abscess most often follows biliary disease, as enteric bacteria such as E. coli and Klebsiella ascend from the obstructed duct.
Exclude amebic abscess, which needs exposure in an endemic area and yields sterile, anchovy-paste fluid.
questions.why: Pyogenic liver abscess most often follows biliary obstruction. Stagnant bile above a stone becomes infected by enteric gram-negative rods, such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and raised pressure in the ducts pushes bacteria into the liver, where they form one or several abscesses. Other routes include the portal vein from abdominal infection, such as diverticulitis, and the hepatic artery during bacteremia. Amebic liver abscess, in contrast, follows Entamoeba histolytica colitis in someone from or returning from an endemic area, and its aspirate is sterile, reddish brown fluid.
whyNot: Entamoeba histolytica reaches the liver through the portal vein from colonic ulcers, usually after travel to or residence in an endemic area, and its aspirate is sterile anchovy-paste fluid.
Staphylococcus aureus can seed the liver through the hepatic artery during bacteremia from a distant site, while this patient has an infected bile duct and cultures growing a gram-negative rod.
Correct.
Echinococcus granulosus forms a slowly enlarging hydatid cyst after ingestion of eggs from dog feces, without acute sepsis.

questions.stem: During endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography to remove the stone, contrast shows that most of the pancreas drains through the minor duodenal papilla, separate from the bile duct. Failure of which of the following developmental events explains this finding?
options: Rotation of the ventral bud around the duodenum
Fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts
Recanalization of the solid duodenal lumen
Outgrowth of the hepatic diverticulum from the foregut
approach: Recall that the pancreas forms from a dorsal bud and a ventral bud, each with its own duct.
Normally the ventral duct joins the distal dorsal duct to form the main pancreatic duct, which opens with the bile duct at the major papilla.
If the ducts do not fuse, the dorsal duct drains most of the gland through the minor papilla: pancreas divisum.
questions.why: The pancreas forms from two buds of foregut endoderm. The dorsal bud forms most of the gland, and the ventral bud, which arises beside the bile duct, rotates with it behind the duodenum to form the uncinate process and lower head. Normally the ventral duct joins the distal part of the dorsal duct to form the main pancreatic duct, which drains with the bile duct at the major papilla. When the ducts fail to fuse (pancreas divisum), most of the gland drains through the dorsal duct and the minor papilla. Abnormal migration of the ventral bud around both sides of the duodenum causes annular pancreas.
whyNot: Abnormal migration of the ventral bud, with tissue passing around both sides of the duodenum, produces annular pancreas, which encircles and can narrow the duodenum.
Correct.
Failed recanalization of the duodenum causes duodenal atresia, which presents in newborns.
The hepatic diverticulum gives rise to the liver, gallbladder, and extrahepatic bile ducts and does not form pancreatic ducts.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her long course of total parenteral nutrition led to gallstone formation?
options: No enteral fat to trigger cholecystokinin release
Increased secretin-driven dilution of hepatic bile
Loss of active sodium absorption by gallbladder epithelium
Increased bile acid synthesis lowering bile cholesterol
approach: Recall that cholecystokinin, released by duodenal I cells when fat and protein arrive, contracts the gallbladder.
With nothing entering the gut, CCK stays low and the gallbladder rarely empties.
Bile then sits in the gallbladder while its epithelium keeps absorbing sodium and water, so it becomes concentrated and forms sludge and stones.
questions.why: Between meals the gallbladder stores bile and concentrates it by actively absorbing sodium, with chloride and water following. After a meal, CCK from duodenal I cells contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, and the gallbladder empties. During total parenteral nutrition no food reaches the duodenum, so CCK stays low and the gallbladder hardly empties. Prolonged stasis and ongoing concentration let mucus, cholesterol crystals, and calcium bilirubinate form sludge, which often progresses to stones.
whyNot: Correct.
Secretin adds bicarbonate-rich fluid to bile, which would dilute it, and its release falls when no meals enter the gut.
Gallbladder sodium absorption continues during fasting; its loss would leave bile dilute and less likely to form stones.
More bile acid synthesis would keep more cholesterol in micelles and lower the risk of stones.

dx: Black pigment gallstones in a teenager with sickle cell disease and Gilbert syndrome
case: A 16-year-old girl with sickle cell disease (hemoglobin SS) comes to the physician because of 2 months of recurrent right upper quadrant pain after meals. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Her sclerae are icteric, and the right upper quadrant is mildly tender. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL (12 to 16), reticulocyte count of 14% (0.5 to 2.5), lactate dehydrogenase of 610 U/L (140 to 280), total bilirubin of 5.9 mg/dL (0.1 to 1.2), and direct bilirubin of 0.3 mg/dL (0 to 0.3). Ultrasonography shows multiple small gallstones, and several are visible on a plain radiograph. Diagnosis: black pigment gallstones in sickle cell disease with coexisting Gilbert syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how her gallstones formed?
options: Bacterial deconjugation of bilirubin in infected ducts
Excess bilirubin in bile precipitating as calcium salts
Cholesterol supersaturation from estrogen-driven secretion
Gallbladder stasis from absent cholecystokinin release
approach: Link chronic hemolysis (anemia, high reticulocytes, high LDH, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) to a large bilirubin load.
Recall that excess bilirubin in bile, part of it unconjugated, precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate.
These calcium salts form small, hard, black stones that are often radiopaque.
questions.why: Black pigment stones form in the gallbladder when bile carries an abnormally large load of bilirubin, as in chronic hemolysis or cirrhosis. Some of the bilirubin in bile is unconjugated or only partly conjugated, and this poorly soluble fraction precipitates with calcium as calcium bilirubinate, which polymerizes into hard, black stones. Chronic hemolysis in sickle cell disease is a classic cause, and coexisting Gilbert syndrome adds to the risk. Brown pigment stones form instead in infected bile ducts, where bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin.
whyNot: Bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugating bilirubin in infected ducts forms brown pigment stones, which are linked to biliary infection and parasites.
Correct.
Estrogen raises cholesterol secretion into bile and forms cholesterol stones, which are usually radiolucent and occur with obesity, pregnancy, or rapid weight loss.
Stasis from absent CCK release, as during total parenteral nutrition, promotes sludge; her eating pattern is normal, and her stones reflect a large pigment load from hemolysis.

questions.stem: Her exhaled carbon monoxide concentration is increased, reflecting her rate of heme breakdown. Which of the following steps releases this carbon monoxide?
options: Biliverdin reductase reducing biliverdin
UGT1A1 conjugating bilirubin with glucuronate
Gut bacteria reducing bilirubin to urobilinogen
Heme oxygenase opening the porphyrin ring
approach: Trace heme breakdown in splenic macrophages: heme to biliverdin to bilirubin.
Recall that heme oxygenase opens the porphyrin ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide.
Biliverdin reductase then converts biliverdin to unconjugated bilirubin, which travels to the liver bound to albumin.
questions.why: In macrophages of the spleen and liver, heme oxygenase cleaves the porphyrin ring of heme, releasing iron and one molecule of carbon monoxide and forming green biliverdin. Biliverdin reductase converts biliverdin to unconjugated bilirubin, which binds albumin in plasma. The liver conjugates it with glucuronate through UGT1A1 and secretes it into bile through MRP2, and gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen and stercobilin. Because each heme broken down yields one carbon monoxide molecule, exhaled carbon monoxide rises with the rate of hemolysis.
whyNot: Biliverdin reductase uses NADPH to reduce biliverdin to bilirubin and releases no gas.
UGT1A1 adds glucuronate to bilirubin in hepatocytes, making it water soluble, without releasing carbon monoxide.
Gut bacteria deconjugate and reduce bilirubin to urobilinogen in the intestine; this step releases no carbon monoxide.
Correct.

questions.stem: In contrast, a 30-year-old man with Crohn disease who had 120 cm of terminal ileum resected develops cholesterol gallstones. Which of the following best explains his gallstones?
options: Bile acid pool too small to keep cholesterol soluble
Reduced cholecystokinin output from ileal I cells after resection
Increased hepatic uptake of dietary cholesterol
Accelerated gallbladder emptying after each meal
approach: Recall that about 95% of bile acids are reabsorbed by sodium-coupled transport in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver in portal blood.
Removing the terminal ileum lets bile acids escape into the colon faster than the liver can replace them, so the pool shrinks.
With fewer bile acids, bile cannot hold its cholesterol in micelles, and cholesterol crystals form.
questions.why: Bile acids cycle between the liver and gut several times a day, and active reabsorption in the terminal ileum recovers about 95% of them. After ileal resection or severe ileal disease, bile acids are lost in stool faster than the liver can replace them. Cholesterol stays dissolved in bile only within micelles and vesicles made with bile acids and lecithin, so the bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol and stones form. A large resection like his also causes fat malabsorption with steatorrhea, while smaller resections mainly cause watery bile acid diarrhea.
whyNot: Correct.
I cells are concentrated in the duodenum and jejunum, so an ileal resection does not remove the main source of cholecystokinin.
Dietary cholesterol uptake changes little after ileal resection; the problem is a shortage of bile acids to dissolve cholesterol already in bile.
Faster emptying would reduce stasis and lower the risk of stones.

questions.stem: Her total bilirubin is higher, and almost entirely unconjugated, compared with most patients who have a similar degree of hemolysis. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Complete absence of UGT1A1 activity
Defective canalicular secretion by MRP2
Mildly reduced UGT1A1 transcription in hepatocytes
Impaired hepatocyte storage of conjugated bilirubin
approach: Note that the extra bilirubin is unconjugated, which points to a problem at or before conjugation.
A mild course into adolescence fits a partial loss of UGT1A1, as in Gilbert syndrome, and excludes the complete loss of Crigler-Najjar type I.
With the high bilirubin load of hemolysis, even a modest drop in conjugating capacity raises the serum level and the risk of pigment stones.
questions.why: Gilbert syndrome is most often caused by an extra TA repeat in the TATA box of the UGT1A1 promoter, which lowers expression of the enzyme to roughly 30% of normal. On its own it causes mild, fluctuating unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that rises with fasting, stress, or illness. Combined with the high bilirubin load of chronic hemolysis, the reduced conjugating capacity produces higher serum bilirubin and more pigment gallstones. Crigler-Najjar type I, with absent UGT1A1, causes severe jaundice and kernicterus in infancy, and type II, with partial deficiency, causes a milder course.
whyNot: Complete absence of UGT1A1 is Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I, which causes severe jaundice and kernicterus in the newborn period.
Defective MRP2 is Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which raises conjugated bilirubin and darkens the liver.
Correct.
Impaired hepatic storage and reuptake of conjugated bilirubin is Rotor syndrome, which raises conjugated bilirubin.

dx: Budd-Chiari syndrome with ascites in a woman with polycythemia vera
case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 3 weeks of right upper quadrant pain and increasing abdominal girth. She has polycythemia vera with a JAK2 V617F mutation. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg. There is tender hepatomegaly, shifting dullness, and a palpable spleen tip. Hemoglobin is 17.9 g/dL (12 to 16), and platelet count is 640,000/mm3 (150,000 to 450,000). Paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 2.0 g/dL (1.1 or more indicates portal hypertension) and an ascitic total protein of 3.2 g/dL (2.5 or more is considered high). Doppler ultrasonography shows no flow in the hepatic veins and an enlarged caudate lobe. Diagnosis: Budd-Chiari syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient best indicates that the block causing her portal hypertension is posthepatic rather than prehepatic?
options: A serum-ascites albumin gradient over 1.1 g/dL
Splenomegaly with portosystemic collateral veins
Tender hepatomegaly with high-protein ascites
Elevated hemoglobin and platelet count
approach: Classify the block: prehepatic (portal vein), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis), or posthepatic (hepatic veins, inferior vena cava, right heart).
A posthepatic block congests the sinusoids and the liver itself, so the liver swells and becomes tender and protein-rich fluid leaks from the sinusoids.
A prehepatic block raises pressure only upstream of the liver, so the liver stays normal in size and ascites is less common.
questions.why: Budd-Chiari syndrome is obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, often from thrombosis in people with polycythemia vera or another prothrombotic state. Blood backs up into the sinusoids, which congests and enlarges the liver and stretches its capsule, causing tender hepatomegaly. Sinusoids are leaky, so the ascites is rich in protein, with a high serum-ascites albumin gradient and total protein of 2.5 g/dL or more, a pattern shared with right heart failure. Prehepatic portal vein thrombosis raises portal pressure with a normal-sized liver and causes ascites less often, and cirrhosis gives a high gradient with low-protein ascites.
whyNot: A high gradient shows portal hypertension at any level, prehepatic, intrahepatic, or posthepatic, so it does not locate the block.
Splenomegaly and collateral veins follow raised portal pressure at any level.
Correct.
High hemoglobin and platelets reflect polycythemia vera, the cause of her thrombosis, and do not locate the block.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy shows congestion and necrosis of hepatocytes around the central veins. Occlusion of a single inflow vessel to the liver rarely causes infarction. Which of the following best explains why outflow obstruction injured her liver?
options: Portal and arterial blood share the same hepatic vein outflow
The hepatic artery supplies most of the blood that enters the liver
Portal venous blood arrives with almost no oxygen left in it
Hepatocytes beside the portal tracts receive the least oxygen
approach: Recall the dual supply: about 75% of inflow from the portal vein and 25% from the hepatic artery, each providing about half of the oxygen.
Losing one inflow is tolerated because the other still perfuses the sinusoids.
Both streams mix in the sinusoids and leave through the central and hepatic veins, so blocking outflow stagnates all of it, starting in zone 3 around the central veins.
questions.why: The liver receives about three quarters of its blood from the portal vein and one quarter from the hepatic artery, and each supplies roughly half of its oxygen. Because two separate inflows feed the same sinusoids, occlusion of one rarely causes infarction. Both inflows, however, drain through the central veins into the hepatic veins. When the hepatic veins thrombose, flow through the whole lobule stagnates, and zone 3 hepatocytes around the central veins, which already receive the least oxygenated blood, become congested and die first.
whyNot: Correct.
About 75% of hepatic blood flow comes from the portal vein, and the hepatic artery supplies the remaining quarter.
Portal blood is partly deoxygenated after passing through the gut and spleen, yet it still supplies about half of the oxygen the liver receives.
Hepatocytes beside the portal tracts (zone 1) receive the best oxygenated blood; zone 3 cells near the central veins receive the least.

topics: Dual blood supply of the liver

questions.stem: Her urine sodium concentration is 8 mEq/L (under 20 indicates avid renal sodium retention), even though her total body sodium is increased. Which of the following best explains her renal sodium retention?
options: Primary aldosterone excess from an adrenal adenoma
Suppressed renin release caused by an expanded plasma volume
Increased ANP release from stretched cardiac atria
Splanchnic vasodilation lowering effective arterial volume
approach: Recall that portal hypertension causes splanchnic arterial vasodilation, largely through nitric oxide.
Pooling of blood in the dilated splanchnic bed lowers the effective arterial blood volume sensed by baroreceptors and the kidney.
The body responds with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation, sympathetic activation, and ADH release, so the kidneys retain sodium and water, which feeds the ascites.
questions.why: In portal hypertension, nitric oxide and other vasodilators widen the splanchnic arteries. Blood pools in this bed, so the effective arterial volume falls even though total body sodium and water are increased. Baroreceptors and the juxtaglomerular apparatus respond with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation, sympathetic activation, and ADH release. The kidneys retain sodium and water, plasma volume expands, and high sinusoidal pressure pushes the extra fluid into the peritoneal cavity. A serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more confirms that the ascites comes from portal hypertension.
whyNot: An aldosterone-secreting adenoma causes hypertension and hypokalemia with suppressed renin, and escape from its sodium-retaining effect prevents edema and ascites.
An expanded plasma volume would suppress renin and increase sodium excretion; in portal hypertension renin is high because the effective arterial volume is low.
Atrial natriuretic peptide increases sodium excretion, so more of it would raise urine sodium.
Correct.

questions.stem: Upper endoscopy shows varices in the distal esophagus. Blood flowing through these varices returns to the systemic circulation mainly through which of the following veins?
options: Inferior mesenteric vein
Azygos vein
Superficial epigastric vein
Left gonadal vein
approach: Identify the anastomosis: the left gastric vein (portal) connects with esophageal veins (systemic) at the distal esophagus.
Follow the systemic side: esophageal veins drain into the azygos system and then the superior vena cava.
When portal pressure rises, blood flows through this connection in reverse and dilates the submucosal veins into varices.
questions.why: Portal hypertension forces portal blood through connections with systemic veins. At the distal esophagus, the left gastric vein, a portal tributary, connects with esophageal veins that drain into the azygos vein and then the superior vena cava. These submucosal veins dilate into varices that can rupture and bleed massively. Other portosystemic anastomoses link the paraumbilical veins with abdominal wall veins, producing caput medusae, and the superior rectal vein with the middle and inferior rectal veins, producing anorectal varices.
whyNot: The inferior mesenteric vein is part of the portal system, so blood in it is still on the portal side.
Correct.
The superficial epigastric veins receive portal blood from the paraumbilical veins and form caput medusae on the abdominal wall.
The left gonadal vein drains to the left renal vein and has no role in esophageal varices.
